    Jelly-RDF 1.1 vs 1.2

    Jelly-RDF 1.2 features a new column layout for stream frames, which improves throughput and reduces serialized size (see the changes from Jelly-RDF 1.1). The first versions to support it are Jelly-JVM 4.0.0 and pyjelly 0.9.0. Both also include other performance improvements in the implementation itself that made Jelly-RDF 1.1 faster as well. This page compares Jelly-RDF 1.2 with Jelly-RDF 1.1, and also shows the performance improvements coming from the implementations.

    The charts are interactive – hover over them for details.

    Jump to:

    • Jelly-JVM – Apache Jena and Eclipse RDF4J
    • pyjelly – RDFLib and the generic API

    Jelly-JVM

    Benchmark setup

    The same datasets, hardware, software, and method were used as in the Jelly-RDF benchmarks, with the "big" preset. Three versions were compared:

    • 3.7 (Jelly-RDF 1.1) – Jelly-JVM 3.7.3, Jelly-RDF 1.1, frame size 256
    • 4.0 (Jelly-RDF 1.1) – Jelly-JVM 4.0.0 writing Jelly-RDF 1.1, frame size 1024
    • 4.0 (Jelly-RDF 1.2) – Jelly-JVM 4.0.0, Jelly-RDF 1.2, frame size 1024

    Each of the three versions was run 6 times for every dataset. The result for a dataset is the median of the 6 runs.

    Why are Jelly-RDF 1.1 files smaller on Jelly-JVM 4.0?

    Jelly-JVM 4.0 changed the prefix and name ID assignment algorithm to favor allocating long runs of consecutive IDs, instead of spreading them randomly. This reduces the number of "noisy" IDs which helps with zstd compression, and also allows us to skip writing some prefix and name IDs thanks to delta compression. Such better-compressed files can still be read by existing Jelly-RDF 1.1 readers.

    pyjelly

    Benchmark setup

    The same datasets, hardware, software, and method were used as in the pyjelly Jelly-RDF benchmarks, with pyjelly's streaming API and the "big" preset. Throughput was measured with RDFLib terms and with the terms of pyjelly's generic API, which does not use RDFLib. Three versions were compared:

    • 0.8 (Jelly-RDF 1.0) – pyjelly 0.8.2, Jelly-RDF 1.0, frame size 250 (its defaults)
    • 0.9 (Jelly-RDF 1.1) – pyjelly 0.9.0 writing Jelly-RDF 1.1, frame size 1024
    • 0.9 (Jelly-RDF 1.2) – pyjelly 0.9.0, Jelly-RDF 1.2, frame size 1024

    Each of the three versions was run 6 times for every dataset. The result for a dataset is the median of the 6 runs. Serialized sizes are from the RDFLib integration (the generic API writes the same bytes in 0.9.0, and within 3% of them in 0.8.2).
